1100.title: Virtue without trying
1100.hook: the highest virtue doesn't try to be virtuous, and so has virtue (Tao Te Ching 38)
1100.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-eight as a warning against goodness as performance, valuing the kindness that comes naturally over rules and appearances.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was doing nothing: the Tao doesn't force, and so nothing is left undone. Your line was nothing undone.

A paper grocery bag splits on the sidewalk, and oranges roll everywhere. Before anyone has decided anything, a teenager with headphones is already crouched down, chasing one into the gutter. Hands it back, nods, walks on. No speech. No look-at-me. Ask about it later and there'd probably be a shrug. By tradition, yesterday's chapter closed the first part of the Tao Te Ching, the part on the Tao. Chapter thirty-eight opens the second part, with today's word, and it starts with a riddle about exactly that kind of kindness.
screen: `A SPLIT BAG, ORANGES EVERYWHERE.` → `HELP BEFORE ANY DECIDING.` → `THE SECOND PART BEGINS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. De, written 德, is the Te in Tao Te Ching. In English it's given as virtue, but not in the sense of a list of rules. It's closer to the power or quality something has when it's in tune with the Tao. Second, the riddle. The chapter says the highest de doesn't try to be de, and that's why it has it. The lower kind never lets go of being virtuous, and that's why it falls short. The teenager with the oranges isn't thinking, I am a kind person. The kindness just happens. The moment it becomes a performance, something thins out. Third, the ladder down. The chapter traces a slide. When the Tao is lost, de comes after. When de is lost, benevolence. When benevolence is lost, righteousness. When righteousness is lost, propriety, the rules of proper form. And propriety, it says, is the thin edge of loyalty and good faith, and the beginning of disorder. Each step is a little more effort and a little less real. Fourth, the fruit. The chapter ends by saying the great person stays with what is thick, not what is thin, with the fruit and not the flower. Back on the sidewalk, that's the difference between kindness and looking kind. One is the orange handed back. The other is the post about handing it back. The chapter isn't against good manners. It's pointing underneath them, to the thing manners were trying to copy.

Your line: without trying. Kindness that doesn't stop to admire itself. Go gently.

1101.title: Rooted in the humble
1101.hook: the high is rooted in the low; nobility rests on humility (Tao Te Ching 39)
1101.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty-nine as a reminder that anything high depends on what is low, and practice humility by honoring plain work and the people who do it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was de: the highest virtue doesn't try to be virtuous. Your line was without trying.

In chapter thirty-nine of the Tao Te Ching, kings call themselves by lowly names. The chapter says princes and rulers call themselves the orphaned, the lonely, the unworthy. Not the mighty. Not the glorious. The ones at the very top of the ladder choose names from the very bottom of it. Odd, until you see what the chapter is building. It starts in the sky and works its way down to the ground, and it ends with a plain stone. By tradition it belongs to the book's part on de, and it's about where height comes from.
screen: `KINGS TAKE LOWLY NAMES.` → `ORPHANED, LONELY, UNWORTHY.` → `WHERE HEIGHT COMES FROM.`

segments.voice: First, the One. The chapter opens with a list of things that have attained the One, which Legge explains as the Tao. Heaven, by it, is clear. Earth, by it, is steady. Spirits have their power from it, valleys are full, living things are alive, and rulers set the pattern for everyone else. Each has its best quality from something it didn't make. Second, without it. The chapter runs the list again in reverse. Without what makes it clear, heaven would crack. Without what makes it steady, earth would shake. Valleys would run dry, living things would perish, rulers would fall. Nothing on the list holds itself up. Third, the root. Here's the heart of it, paraphrased: the noble takes the lowly as its root, and the high takes the low as its foundation. That's why kings, the chapter says, call themselves orphaned, lonely, unworthy. They're naming what they stand on. Fourth, the stone. The chapter ends with two materials. It doesn't want to glitter like jade. It would rather be plain and rough, like an ordinary stone. Outside the palace, the high things in a life stand on something low. The person at the top of a company stands on people who clean the building at night. A good dinner stands on someone washing pans. A healthy body stands on sleep and water and feet. The chapter's kings remember that out loud, in their own names.

1102.title: The way returns
1102.hook: returning is the movement of the Tao; yielding is its way (Tao Te Ching 40)
1102.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty as a picture of the way moving in cycles, and some treat a return to an abandoned practice or relationship as part of that movement rather than a failure.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was rooted in the humble: the high stands on the low, the way a tree stands on what's underground. Your line was rooted low.

A swing goes forward as far as it can, hangs at the top for half a second, and comes back. Nobody calls that a failure. The coming back is how it gets to go forward again. A tide runs out across the sand and returns. A breath goes out, and the next one comes in. Chapter forty of the Tao Te Ching is short, and it opens on exactly this motion: the way things go out, and the way they come home.
screen: `A SWING GOES OUT AND COMES BACK.` → `A TIDE, A BREATH.` → `CHAPTER FORTY.`

segments.voice: First, the line. James Legge set the opening as a little verse: "The movement of the Tao By contraries proceeds; And weakness marks the course Of Tao's mighty deeds." Legge heard contraries: things turning toward their opposites. Other translators render the same opening as returning: the way moves by coming back. Some readers hear both at once. What grows full turns toward empty; what goes out comes home. Second, where it returns to. Chapter sixteen spoke of all things returning to their root, and chapter forty ends on the same note: everything under heaven comes from being, and being comes from non-being. So the return isn't only a swing back and forth. It's a coming home to where things started. Third, the other half: weakness marks the course. The way doesn't shove. It yields, the way water gives ground and still finds its level. Returning and yielding sit side by side, like one motion seen from two angles. Fourth, closer to home. A lot of life is arranged around going out: further, faster, more. Chapter forty quietly suggests that turning back is part of the movement, not a break in it. Coming back to a friend you drifted from. Picking up a book you set down halfway. Returning to a practice after weeks away. In this reading, returning isn't starting over. It's how the way moves.
screen: `CONTRARIES, OR RETURNING.` · `HOME TO THE ROOT.` · `WEAKNESS MARKS THE COURSE.` · `COMING BACK ISN'T STARTING OVER.` · then, large: `THE WAY RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that you once did and then set down: a walk you used to take, a person you meant to write to, an instrument in a closet, a prayer if you pray, or a quiet morning hour if you don't. Don't scold yourself for the gap; just turn toward it, the way a breath turns and comes back in. Let your breathing do the teaching: out, a pause, and back.
The way returns. Chapter forty's movement: the Tao goes out and comes back, and it yields as it goes. Today's word.
Your line: returning. Coming back isn't the opposite of going forward. That's today, done.

1103.title: If they didn't laugh
1103.hook: when the foolish hear of the Tao they laugh, and without their laughter it wouldn't be the Tao (Tao Te Ching 41)
1103.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often quote chapter forty-one when a practice like stillness or simplicity draws puzzled looks, taking the laugh as part of the path rather than a reason to quit.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the way returns: the Tao goes out and comes back, and yields as it goes. Your line was returning.

Someone at work sees you sit with your eyes closed for a minute at your desk and asks, half joking, whether you've fallen asleep. Or a cousin at a family dinner raises an eyebrow at the morning walk, the candle, the phone left in another room. A small laugh. Not cruel, just puzzled. Chapter forty-one of the Tao Te Ching saw that laugh coming, and it treats the laugh as something other than a problem.
screen: `EYES CLOSED AT A DESK.` → `A PUZZLED LAUGH.` → `CHAPTER FORTY-ONE SAW IT COMING.`

segments.voice: First, three hearers. The chapter opens with three kinds of people hearing about the way. The first hears and puts it into practice with everything they have. The second seems to keep it one day and lose it the next. The third laughs out loud. Second, the twist. In James Legge's translation the chapter says of that laugh: "If it were not (thus) laughed at, it would not be fit to be the Tao." The laugh is treated almost as a sign. If the way made perfect sense to everyone at first glance, it wouldn't be the way. Third, why it looks funny. The chapter goes straight on to things that look like their opposites: the bright way seems dim, the way forward seems to go back, the level way seems rough. Seen from outside, slowing down looks like falling behind, and sitting still looks like doing nothing. And the chapter doesn't tell anyone to argue with the laughers, or to look down on them. The laugh comes with the territory. Fourth, the middle hearer. Keeping a practice for a week, then dropping it the first time somebody smirks: that's the middle hearer's pattern. Chapter forty-one offers that hearer something steadying. The laugh doesn't prove you're wrong. It may only prove that what you're doing looks, from outside, like nothing.
screen: `THREE HEARERS.` · `NO LAUGH, NO TAO.` · `IT LOOKS LIKE ITS OPPOSITE.` · `THE MIDDLE HEARER.` · then, large: `IF THEY DIDN'T LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Settle where you are, and if anyone near you could see, let them see. Let a little self-consciousness rise, the feeling of being watched doing something that looks like nothing, and keep sitting through it without pushing it away. If you pray, this can be a quiet prayer; if you don't, two minutes of breathing on purpose.
If they didn't laugh. Chapter forty-one: when some people hear of the way, they laugh, and if they didn't, it wouldn't be the way. Today's word.
Your line: they laugh. A puzzled smile is no verdict on a quiet minute. See you tomorrow.

1104.title: One, two, three
1104.hook: the Tao produced one, one two, two three, three all things; all carry yin and embrace yang (Tao Te Ching 42)
1104.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-two's yin and yang as a picture of opposites held together in balance, and some use it as a reminder not to cling to one side of a pair.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was if they didn't laugh: some hear of the way and laugh, and if they didn't, it wouldn't be the way. Your line was they laugh.

One, two, three. It's how a child counts before jumping into a pool, how a band counts in a song, how a race begins. Chapter forty-two of the Tao Te Ching counts too, and in a handful of words it gets from the way to everything there is. Right after the counting, it names two words that have traveled far beyond the book, onto t-shirts and tattoos and necklaces split in half: yin and yang. Here they are, where this chapter puts them.
screen: `ONE, TWO, THREE.` → `FROM THE WAY TO EVERYTHING.` → `YIN AND YANG, IN THEIR SETTING.`

segments.voice: First, the count. In James Legge's translation: "The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three; Three produced All things." It reads like a family tree, or a seed becoming a forest. Second, the honest part. The chapter never says what one, two and three are. Some readers take one as the first unity, two as yin and yang, and three as what happens when the two blend. Others leave the numbers as a rhythm: from one, many. The text stays quiet, and it's fine to let it. Third, the two words. All things, the chapter says, carry yin on their backs and hold yang in their arms, and a blending breath brings them into harmony. Legge doesn't even write yin and yang; he renders them as the Obscurity and the Brightness. Either way, the picture isn't a fight between good and bad. Every single thing carries both at once, and the harmony comes from the blend, not from one side winning. Fourth, in a single day. It's easy to sort a day into opposites and want only one side: rest and not work, praise and not criticism, sunshine and not shade. The chapter's picture is gentler. Effort and ease in the same breath. Strength and tenderness in the same person. A sad morning and a good afternoon in the same day. The work isn't to get rid of one. It's to let the two find their balance.

segments.voice: Breathe in, then out: neither one is the good one, and you need both. Look around for light and shadow side by side, then check your body for somewhere tense and somewhere soft. Don't fix either; just notice that both are there at once, and let the breath move between them.
Yin yang. In chapter forty-two, the two that every single thing carries at once, brought into harmony by a blending breath. Today's word.
Your line: carry both. Nothing has to win for the day to be whole. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1105.title: The softest thing
1105.hook: the softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest (Tao Te Ching 43)
1105.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often turn to chapter forty-three's image of water on stone when a situation won't yield to force, choosing steady, gentle persistence instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was yin yang: every single thing carries both, and a blending breath brings them into harmony. Your line was carry both.

Under an old gutter spout, the concrete has a shallow bowl worn into it. Nobody chiseled it. Nobody planned it. Rain did it, one drop after another, season after season, on the same patch of ground. The concrete is harder than any raindrop. The concrete still lost. Chapter forty-three of the Tao Te Ching opens on that kind of quiet victory, and then it adds something new.
screen: `A BOWL WORN INTO CONCRETE.` → `NOBODY CHISELED IT.` → `RAIN DID.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In James Legge's translation, chapter forty-three begins: "The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the hardest." Last week, chapter thirty-six said the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong. This chapter says it again, then goes somewhere new. Second, the new thing. What has no substance, it says, can enter where there is no crack at all. Water doesn't need a door. It finds its way into the stone, the soil, the root. The softest thing doesn't win by smashing through. It gets in where nothing hard could. Third, a way of teaching. The chapter says this shows the benefit of not forcing, and it speaks of a teaching without words. Then it adds, plainly, that few in the world reach it. That's an honest admission inside the book itself: this is hard to live. Fourth, the hard places in a life. A teenager who won't talk. A coworker braced for an argument. An old family wound. Pushing harder doesn't always open them. The chapter's picture is different: steady, gentle, repeated presence, the way rain keeps falling on the same spot. A kind word every day. A meal left without comment. In this reading, the soft way doesn't break the stone. It gets in.
screen: `THE SOFTEST OVERCOMES THE HARDEST.` · `IT ENTERS WHERE THERE'S NO CRACK.` · `A TEACHING WITHOUT WORDS.` · `STEADY, GENTLE, REPEATED.` · then, large: `THE SOFTEST THING.`

segments.voice: If you can, let a thin stream of water run over a pebble, a spoon or the back of your hand; if not, close your eyes and picture a river over rocks, or rain on a step. Watch how the water doesn't argue with what's in its way: it goes around, over, into. Let your breath move like that, soft and steady, without pushing.
The softest thing. Chapter forty-three: the softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest, and enters where there is no crack. Today's word.
Your line: the softest. Rain never hurries, and still the stone gives way to it. Until tomorrow.

1106.title: Which is dearer?
1106.hook: fame or your life, which is dearer? know contentment and avoid disgrace (Tao Te Ching 44)
1106.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often use chapter forty-four's question, fame or life, as a check on chasing recognition or money at the cost of health, rest and the people around them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the softest thing: it overcomes the hardest, and gets in where there's no crack. Your line was the softest.

Late at night, a phone lights up a face in a dark room. Refresh. How many people saw the post? Refresh. Did anyone new follow? An hour goes by that could have been sleep, or a talk with someone in the next room, or nothing at all. Nobody chose to trade the hour. It just went. Chapter forty-four of the Tao Te Ching doesn't scold anyone for this. It asks a question instead, and leaves it standing there.
screen: `A PHONE AT MIDNIGHT.` → `REFRESH, REFRESH.` → `AN HOUR, TRADED.`

segments.voice: First, the question. James Legge set chapter forty-four in rhyme, and it opens: "Or fame or life, Which do you hold more dear? Or life or wealth, To which would you adhere?" The chapter doesn't answer for you. Second, the trade. Great attachment, it says, brings great cost, and piling things up leads to heavy loss. It isn't saying a name or money is evil. It's pointing at the trade underneath: what you spend of your actual life to get them. Third, the way out it offers. Whoever knows contentment avoids disgrace. Whoever knows when to stop avoids danger, and can last a long time. Those aren't prizes at the end. They're the brakes on the trade. Fourth, fame at a small scale. It can be a few more likes, the boss's notice, being the one who always says yes. Each of those costs something: an evening, an hour of sleep, a weekend with someone you love. The question isn't a rule. It's a weighing. And this is the end of a week, so here is what it gathered: without trying, rooted low, returning, they laugh, carry both, the softest, and today, which is dearer. Small, quiet strengths that can look like weakness from outside.
screen: `OR FAME OR LIFE?` · `WHAT YOU SPEND TO GET IT.` · `KNOW WHEN TO STOP.` · `A WEEK OF QUIET STRENGTHS.` · then, large: `WHICH IS DEARER?`

segments.voice: Let one small chase come to mind, something you do to be seen, praised or counted, and hold it in one hand. In the other, hold what it costs: sleep, time with someone, quiet, your attention. Don't decide anything yet; just feel the weight in each hand.
Which is dearer? Chapter forty-four's question: fame or your life, wealth or your life. Whoever knows contentment avoids disgrace. Today's word.
Your line: which is dearer. A question to hold, not a rule to keep. That's the week.
